## What is menopause? 

\begin{itemize}
\item When menstruation pauses (stops) \pause
\item Officially in menopause when you have gone 12 months without menstruating
\begin{itemize}
\item The time leading up to menopause is called peri-menopause 
\item After the 12-month mark, you are "menopausal" or postmenopausal \pause 
\end{itemize}
\item What happens? \pause
\begin{itemize}
\item How much did you know about menopause before reading? 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## "Symptoms" in Menopause and Peri-menopause 

\begin{itemize}
\item Referring to the experiences during (peri-)menopause as symptoms is in itself controversial \pause
\begin{itemize}
\item Because menopause is not a "disease" \pause
\item But we will use "symptoms" to describe the physical and mental health experiences attributable to menopause \pause 
\end{itemize}
\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
\item diminished sleep quality 
\item insomnia
\item irritability 
\item depression
\item mood swings
\item difficulty concentrating 
\item reduced quality of life 
\item aching joints
\item bloating 
\item breast tenderness 
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.5\textwidth} 
\item bladder/urinary discomfort
\item more frequent urinary tract infections 
\item vaginal dryness, discharge, and bleeding 
\item loss of sexual desire, painful intercourse
\item headaches
\item thinning hair 
\item heart palpitations
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{itemize}

## Menopausal Hormone Therapy: History
\begin{itemize}
\item What is (o)estrogen? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Everyone has hormones! Everyone has estrogen(s)-- different types and different quantities \pause 
\item In females, primarily produced in ovaries and placenta (when pregnant); responsible for development and regulation of female reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics \pause
\end{itemize}
\item 1940s: new techniques to extract estrogen from the urine of pregnant mares (female horses); marketed as a treatment for menopausal symptoms in the 1950s \pause
\item 1960s: "Feminine Forever": youth, beauty, full sex life for menopausal women who take estrogen \pause
\item 1980s: Progesterone added for women with uterus as estrogen alone increased rates of uterine cancer and endometrial cancer (estrogen alone still used for those without uterus)
\end{itemize}

## Hormone "Replacement" Therapy 
\begin{itemize}
\item 1970s: Criticism of "paternalistic" medical establishment labeling menopause as a "deficiency disease" when it is a natural part of aging \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item 2000s: some argue girls do well until puberty, spend decades on an emotional and physical roller coaster, then even out. Menopause is not a deficiency: women suffer from "estrogen posioning" between puberty and menopause \pause
\end{itemize}

\item 1980s-1990s: multiple observational studies suggest hormones (estrogen or estrogen+progesterone) reduce risk of heart disease, reduce development of osteoporosis, might reduce the risk of Alzheimer's, and are the best available treatment for vasomotor symptoms \pause
\begin{itemize}
\item "...estrogen should be in the water... we thought it was like fluoride" -Hadine Joffe, Harvard Medical School professor of psychiatry 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## The Women's Health Initiative 
\begin{itemize}
\item under the National Institutes of Health (NIH)
\item Launched in 1993 
\item Aims: test the benefits and risks of hormonal therapies (estrogen or estrogen+progesterone) for chronic diseases \pause

\item 16608 women without hysterectomy (intact uterus) randomized: 8506 assigned to estrogen+progesterone (CEE+MPA), 8102 assigned to placebo \pause 

\item Intervention phase: November 1993-July 2002 \pause 

\item Study halted July 2002 (average follow-up 5.2 years)

\end{itemize}

## WHI Halted 
\begin{itemize}
\item Why did the WHI halt the estrogen+progesterone arm of the study in 2002? \pause \item Increased risks of breast cancer, stroke, heart attack, and clots (pulmonary embolism) \pause 
\item What do we mean by increased risks? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item In 1 year for 10,000 postmenopausal women taking estrogen+progesterone, 8 more will have invasive breast cancer, 7 more will have a heart attack, 8 more will have a stroke, 18 more will have blood clots, than a similar group of 10,000 women not taking the hormones (Dr. Rossouw, acting director WHI)
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## WHI Criticized
\begin{itemize}
\item The halt? Internal Validity? External Validity? \pause
\item Criticism of the halt: at the time (July 2002), differences in risks across treatment and control groups not statistically significant \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item How many additional cases of breast cancer is too many? \pause
\end{itemize}
\item Internal validity: \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item High numbers of past/current hormone users (current users had a 3 month wash-out period) \pause 
\item No multiple outcomes, multiple subgroup comparison adjustments \pause 
\end{itemize}
\item External validity: \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item "healthy women" \pause
\item application of results to peri-menopausal women \pause
\item contextualization of risks 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## Risk as an Estimand 
\begin{itemize}
\item Why is difference in means inappropriate? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Time is a factor (longitudinal): (a) women who did not have breast cancer at t=1 might develop it at t=2 or t=5, (b) the numerator at t=5 may be different as people die \pause 
\end{itemize}
\item Survival Analysis and Hazard Ratios 
\begin{itemize}
\item relate time that passes before an event occurs (e.g. breast cancer, stroke, death) to covariates \pause 
\item WHI study uses Cox proportional hazard models: every disease/outcome has an underlying hazard function that changes over time (such as the risk of heart attack increases over time), $\lambda_0(t)$, combined with hazards based on an individual's covariates (weight, smoker, exercise, \textbf{treatment status}) \pause
\item Hazard ratio of treatment $D$: $\frac{\lambda(t|D=1)}{\lambda(t|D=0)} = \frac{\lambda_0(t) \ exp(\beta_1 \cdot 1)}{\lambda_0(t) \ exp(\beta_1 \cdot 0)} = exp(\beta_1)$
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## Risk as an Estimand 
\begin{itemize}
\item How do we interpret hazard ratios? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item What if $HR=1$? \pause no difference between the hazard of heart attack for treatment and control \pause 
\item What if $HR<1$? \pause hazard of heart attack is lower for treated \pause 
\item What if $HR>1$? \pause hazard of heart attack is higher for treated \pause
\end{itemize}
\item In 2002, the WHI Data and Safety Monitoring Board calculated an HR of 1.26, a 26\% increase in breast cancer risk under treatment \pause 
\item The WHI and media reporting on the halt of the study have been criticized for failing to communicate the difference between absolute and relative risks ($\frac{8}{10000} \neq .26$)
\end{itemize}

## Results from WHI (and WHIMS)

What is the effect of estrogren+progesterone on invasive breast cancer in post-menopausal women? 

\begin{itemize}
\item Intervention phase (1993-2002): HR of 1.24 (95\% CI, 1.01-1.53) \pause
\item  9 more cases of invasive breast cancer per 10,000 person-years 
\end{itemize}

## Results from WHI (and WHIMS)
\begin{itemize}
\item Cumulative follow-up: HR 1.28 (95\% CI, 1.11-1.48); risk attenuation with time since cessation of hormone therapy use 
\end{itemize}

## Results from WHI(MS)
\begin{itemize}
\item Who enrolled in WHIMS? \pause 65 to 79 year olds, free of dementia at the time of enrollment \pause CEE+MPA Arm: 2131 assigned to treatment, 2213 placebo; mean follow-up 4.2 years \pause
\item What is the outcome of interest? \pause Annual measure of 3MSE (cognition test) scored 0 to 100 \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Temporal and spatial orientation, immediate and delayed recall, executive function, naming, verbal fluency, abstract reasoning, writing, copying \pause 
\item Women who scored below cutpoints were given additional testing for dementia (follow ups continued regardless of dementia status) \pause
\end{itemize}
\item We still have longitudinal challenge: first-order autoregressive structure  
\end{itemize}

## Results from WHI(MS)
\begin{itemize}
\item In treatment and placebo groups, 3MSE scores increase over time (first 4 years) \pause
\item Why is adherence a concern? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Non-compliance is always a concern to some extent, but non-compliance here may be directly related to cognitive decline! \pause
\end{itemize}
\item CEE+MPA difference from placebo averaged 0.18 points (SE 0.10) \pause
\item Difference is "too small to have relevance in clinical practice" 

\end{itemize}

## Recent Observational Studies 

\begin{itemize}
\item What concerns us about observational studies? \pause 
\item Why consider evidence from observational studies? \pause 

\item Abenhaim et al. 2022: Menopausal Hormone Therapy Formulation and Breast Cancer Risk 
\begin{itemize}
\item Data on over 7 million women in the UK,about 500,000 of which fit age criteria \pause 
\item 43,183 cases of breast cancer, 431,830 matched controls \pause 
\item Different women take different formulations/doses of hormones 
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

## Recent Observational Studies 

\begin{itemize}
\item Kim et al. 2021: Association between menopausal hormone therapy and risk of neurodegenerative diseases: Implications for precision hormone therapy 
\begin{itemize}
\item Data on 1.4 million women from 2007 to 2016 on medical insurance (Humana)
\item 379,352 women met age (over 45) and (propensity score) matching criteria \pause
\item 189,676 used menopausal hormone therapy (treatment), 189,676 did not (control) 
\item Neurodegenerative diseases: Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, dementia, multiple sclerosis, and ALS \pause 
\item Different women use different formulations and administrations 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
